titre: Sex Chromosomes Were Not Discovered by Morgan
accroche: In 1905, two researchers separately discover the sex chromosomes, yet neither of their names remains the most cited
contenu_vulgarise:
In the spring of 1905, in a laboratory of the Carnegie Institution, Nettie Stevens observes under the microscope the reproductive cells of *Tenebrio molitor*, the mealworm beetle. She counts the chromosomes, one by one, on hundreds of preparations.

In males, she finds nineteen large chromosomes of roughly equal size, and a twentieth, distinctly smaller. In females, all twenty chromosomes are large, without exception. Half the sperm carry the small chromosome, the other half do not.

Stevens draws a cautious but clear conclusion: an egg fertilized by a sperm carrying the small chromosome becomes a male; the other, a female. Sex can be read in a structural difference visible under the microscope, not in an invisible, hypothetical factor.

## A discovery by two, almost simultaneous

The same year, a few months apart, Edmund Wilson, already an established professor at Columbia, publishes similar observations on other insects, the hemipterans, in which the extra chromosome is outright absent in the male rather than merely smaller. The two researchers do not work together, but they read each other: Wilson revises his own paper to add, in a note, acknowledgment of Stevens's result on *Tenebrio*.

Neither had, at the outset, the certainty of holding the right explanation. It is the convergence of two independent methods, on different insects, that gives the chromosomal hypothesis of sex its strength.

## The name that stays, and the one that fades

Thomas Hunt Morgan supervised Stevens's thesis at Bryn Mawr, and he is the one most readers today associate with the genetics of the early century: Nobel Prize in 1933, for work with no direct connection to this discovery: the link between a gene and the X chromosome, established later on the fruit fly.

The 1905 episode is not his, however: at the time, Morgan remains skeptical of the chromosomal interpretation of sex, he was already unfavorable to McClung's suggestion in 1901-1902, and he will come around, through other work, his own this time, only shortly after 1910. Credit for that discovery is shared between Stevens and Wilson, though in practice it goes more often to Wilson, an already recognized professor, than to Stevens, whose 1905 monograph today has fewer than a hundred recorded citations.

A founding discovery does not need a single discoverer to be sound. It does need, however, that the story we tell about it not invent one.

repere.texte: In Tenebrio molitor, Nettie Stevens counts twenty chromosomes in the female, all large, versus nineteen large and one small in the male. She publishes this result in 1905, the same year as Edmund Wilson on other insects; her monograph is still cited fewer than a hundred times today.
repere.source: Carey, Aközbek & Harkess, “The contributions of Nettie Stevens to the field of sex chromosome biology,” Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B, 377, 2022

carte.punch: The sex chromosomes were not discovered by the man whose name you remember.
carte.idee: In 1905, Nettie Stevens and Edmund Wilson independently discover that sex can be read in a chromosome, each on different insects. Thomas Hunt Morgan, whom we associate with this period today, had no part in it: his contribution comes from elsewhere, and much later.
carte.source_courte: Carey et al., Phil. Trans. R. Soc. B, 2022

quiz.question: What does Nettie Stevens's 1905 discovery establish that earlier hypotheses about sex determination did not?
choix: That sex depends on a chromosomal difference visible under the microscope, not on an invisible factor
That only females have chromosomes in even numbers
That an insect's sex changes depending on the temperature at which it develops
That Thomas Hunt Morgan had been right from the start about the role of chromosomes
quiz.explication: Stevens shows an observable structural difference (a distinctly smaller chromosome in the male) where earlier hypotheses remained theoretical. Morgan, by contrast, was then opposed to this chromosomal interpretation, which he would adopt only later, through other work.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How does Edmund Wilson's observation in hemipterans differ from Nettie Stevens's in Tenebrio molitor?
choix: In hemipterans, it is the female who carries a chromosome smaller than the male's
In hemipterans, the total number of chromosomes is identical in both sexes
In hemipterans, the extra chromosome is outright absent in the male, rather than merely smaller
Wilson observes no chromosomal difference between the sexes in hemipterans
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The entry distinguishes the two cases: in Tenebrio, the extra chromosome is merely smaller in the male; in the hemipterans Wilson studied, it is simply absent.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Why does the Nobel Prize awarded to Morgan in 1933 not reward the 1905 discovery of the sex chromosomes?
choix: Because Morgan discovered the sex chromosomes alone, without Stevens or Wilson
Because it rewards distinct, later work: the link between a gene and the X chromosome, established in the fruit fly
Because the Nobel committee judged the 1905 discovery non-reproducible
Because Morgan published his own discovery before Stevens and Wilson, as early as 1903
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The 1933 Nobel rewards the link between a gene and the X chromosome, established later in Drosophila, work with no direct connection to the 1905 discovery.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What role did Thomas Hunt Morgan play with Nettie Stevens before the 1905 discovery?
choix: He co-signed with her the 1905 monograph on Tenebrio molitor
He succeeded her as professor at the Carnegie Institution
He funded her research with a personal grant
He supervised her doctoral thesis at Bryn Mawr
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The entry specifies that Morgan supervised Stevens's thesis at Bryn Mawr, before himself remaining skeptical of the chromosomal interpretation of sex for several years.
